approved_claim_dependencies.claim: This Digital Strategy Hub session is useful as public-safe context for community practice around emerging technology, mobile launches, and finance/workflow requests. It does not provide a single product tutorial, but it reinforces that Rock teams should bring concrete use cases to peer review, document what was tried, and separate experimentation from production changes.
Short-form video should be treated as ministry content with a clear next step, not only as entertainment or social promotion.

This Digital Strategy Hub session adds public-safe guidance for evaluating AI search and advanced digital experiences in Rock-backed websites and apps. It highlights the value of intent-based search, mobile and web integration, and careful plugin review before exposing AI-generated responses or search behavior to users.
Emerging technology pilots should stay clearly labeled as experiments until output quality, data boundaries, and ministry usefulness are verified.
Manual curation still matters for sermon and video libraries because view counts alone do not capture pastoral impact, ministry priority, or whether a message should be highlighted again.
Mobile launch and finance work should be tracked as real operational projects with explicit owners, requirements, and verification steps.
AI coaching should be framed as an assisted resource-routing layer with reviewable prompts, ministry-approved categories, and clear human oversight.
Digital content libraries work best when they connect messages, topics, and practical next steps instead of leaving users to browse isolated videos.

When AI summaries are generated from person-profile data, the review should include data minimization, avoidance of direct identifiers, privacy-policy alignment, and vendor assurances about model training.
Online next-step pathways can combine dashboards, content, and LMS when the church defines the discipleship path being supported.

This Digital Strategy Hub session frames AI-assisted coaching and online learning as tools that still need ministry ownership. It connects LMS, dashboards, content, and mobile engagement to a discipleship path, while warning that AI should support reviewed coaching and resource routing rather than make ungoverned ministry decisions.
Peer learning works best when Rock teams bring action-oriented examples, not only abstract tool discussions.

This Digital Strategy Hub session adds public-safe guidance for turning sermon and ministry video libraries into searchable, reusable digital content. It discusses selecting messages by pastoral value and audience response, using platform analytics without over-trusting them, and using AI as a planning aid for titles, categories, and follow-up content rather than as an unreviewed publisher.
Before adopting AI or search plugins, teams should verify data sources, answer boundaries, security behavior, and whether generated results can be reviewed or tuned.

This Digital Strategy Hub presentation provides public-safe guidance for churches evaluating AI. It frames AI as a fast-moving tool category that can assist ministry work, but requires clear use cases, privacy boundaries, staff training, review expectations, and model/vendor awareness before it is connected to Rock data or public-facing experiences.
AI should be introduced around concrete ministry workflows and reviewable outputs, not as a broad replacement for staff judgment.

Episode 202 adds public-safe operational context for Rock release awareness, community-shaped priorities, AI-assisted group matching, and documentation currency; concrete implementation guidance remains tied to official docs, release notes, source code, or live-instance verification.

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: Urgent or culturally timely topics can become good candidates for curated content paths when they are connected to trusted ministry resources and follow-up actions.
AI plugin ideas should be evaluated against real church tasks, content sources, and security expectations rather than adopted because the model capability is new.
Engagement goals should be tied to the path the church wants people to take, not simply to whether a digital tool was launched.
Data analytics meetups can help churches compare dashboards, process designs, and BI-tool choices against real ministry use cases instead of treating reporting as an isolated technical task.

This Digital Strategy Hub session focuses on short-form and on-demand video as part of a broader church digital strategy. It frames video as a way to extend message content, answer timely questions, route people into deeper next steps, and support mobile or web experiences that help people continue engaging after the weekend.
Video analytics are useful for prioritization, but teams should compare them with qualitative feedback and ministry goals before changing content strategy.

For AI-assisted group finding, implementation work needs church-specific matching rules: which group types are findable, which attributes describe affinity, and what boundaries keep the assistant away from inappropriate targets such as security roles.

source_refs.title: Rock's Future Anchored in Vision | Ep 202

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: New website and app experiences should be evaluated together because users may move between public pages, logged-in mobile surfaces, search, profile, and next-step actions.
AI can help draft sermon titles, category ideas, and reuse plans, but churches should keep human review over doctrinal wording, audience fit, and final publication.
Emerging technology and AI experiments should be bounded, documented, and reviewed before they affect Rock data or public ministry workflows.

Use the episode as release-awareness context: podcast release discussion can flag security updates, alpha/beta status, and future model-changing work, but upgrade guidance must still be verified against official release notes and the local Rock version.

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: Attendance-flow analysis can move beyond aggregate weekend counts by classifying engagement patterns, prioritizing follow-up lists, and creating Rock connection requests for campus teams.

The Data Analytics Hub launch frames community analytics as a shared practice space where churches compare dashboards, ministry processes, BI tooling, and Rock-based reporting patterns. The session also includes a Life.Church attendance-flow case study that uses Rock attendance and connection data to prioritize pastoral follow-up while treating AI profile summaries and privacy controls as governance concerns.

Documentation changes should be planned as part of UI and release work; major UI changes can create downstream screenshot and article-refresh work that must be tracked before public guidance is treated as current.

approved_claim_dependencies.claim: AI governance should include staff training, data-minimization rules, and a review path before AI-generated content or data summaries influence public communication or pastoral action.
Because AI model capabilities and vendor terms change quickly, churches should document which tools are approved and what data classes may be used with each one.

Community feedback channels such as Rocket Chat, calls, church visits, and conferences can explain why areas like Connections rise in priority, but agents should treat that as roadmap context rather than proof that a feature is present in a given instance.

Intent-based AI search can improve discovery when it is grounded in approved church content and clearly tested against real user questions.
